title: Why God became man (ST III.1)
hookLine: Thomas speaks of fittingness: nothing more fitting than God sharing our nature

lines: A CARD WOULD HAVE BEEN KIND.
SHE SHOWS UP AT THE DOOR.
cards: Her friend's father has died, across the country. A card would be kind. Flowers would be kind.

Instead she books a flight, takes time off work, and is standing on the porch when the door opens. Nothing required it. But everyone in that house knows it was exactly the right thing, the thing that fit.
Thomas Aquinas opens the third part of his Summa with that kind of question about God. Could God have helped us another way? And if so, why become one of us?

teach.b: Thomas's key word here is fitting. Not necessary. Fitting.
He starts with what God is: goodness itself.
And goodness, Thomas says, following an old Christian writer named Dionysius, is the kind of thing that pours itself out. So it belongs to the highest good to share itself in the highest way.
What higher way than joining a created nature to himself, so that God and a human being are one person? That's the incarnation, God with skin, as day three hundred three put it.
John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Was it necessary? Couldn't God simply have forgiven, by a word?
Thomas says yes, he could have. Nothing forced his hand.
But some things are needed the way a horse is needed for a journey: not because the journey is impossible without it, but because it goes so much better. And this way does more.
It gives faith firmer footing, because God himself is speaking. It gives hope.
It stirs love, because nothing moves a person to love like being loved first. It gives an example to follow. And it opens the door to a surprising gift: sharing in God's own life.
Thomas quotes Augustine's bold line: God became man so that man might become God. Second Peter says: "partakers of the divine nature." So Thomas's answer to why is not a mechanism.
It's a kind of beauty. Of all the ways God might have helped, he sees none that fits better than coming in person and standing at the door.

how: Catholics profess the incarnation in the Creed at Sunday Mass, bowing at the words about Christ becoming man, and kneeling at those words on Christmas and the Annunciation.

games.q: what does “why god became man” mean?
o: as a reward people earned by their good deeds
because God was forced to, to forgive sin
the most fitting way for goodness to share itself

games.q: why God became man — tap the pairs.

s: Thomas says God had no other way to save us
he says God could have forgiven another way. the incarnation was fitting, not forced.
Thomas starts from the idea that goodness shares itself
following Dionysius: the highest good shares itself in the highest way.
Thomas quotes Augustine: God became man so that man might become God
and Second Peter speaks of being partakers of the divine nature.

games.q: a student asks Thomas: couldn't God have simply forgiven the world by a word? what does he answer?
o: no, God had no other option.
yes, but becoming man was the most fitting way.
yes, so the incarnation didn't matter.
games.why: Thomas says God could have done it otherwise. the incarnation was needed like a horse for a journey: not required, but far better.

practice: Look at your own hands for a moment: knuckles, lines, maybe a scar. Christians say God had hands like these, that got tired, and cut, and held people; let that sit without trying to solve it.
If you pray, say the line from John slowly, the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and rest on one word of it; if you don't, simply notice what it would mean to someone to believe that.

wordCard.voice: Why God became man. Thomas's answer: not because God had to, but because, for the highest good, sharing itself in person was the most fitting way. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: fittingness, the way things come together well.

carryVoice: Your line: most fitting. Of all the ways, the one that comes in person. See you tomorrow.
